title: Quicksort
summary: Divide-and-conquer sorting: pick a pivot, partition into elements < pivot and > pivot, recurse. Average O(n log n), worst case O(n^2) (sorted input with naive pivot). In-place (O(log n) stack). Not stable. Randomized pivot gives expected O(n log n). Three-way partition (Dutch national flag) handles duplicates.

structure.meaning: Rearrange array so elements < pivot are left, > pivot are right. Pivot in final position.
Recursively sort left and right partitions.
First/last element (bad for sorted data). Random (expected O(n log n)). Median-of-three (good in practice).
Partition into < pivot, = pivot, > pivot. Handles duplicates efficiently (O(n) for all-equal input).
Quicksort + heapsort fallback. Switches to heapsort if recursion depth exceeds 2*log2(n). Used in C++ std::sort.

notes: Quicksort is the fastest general-purpose sorting algorithm in practice.
Introsort (quicksort + heapsort) is used in C++ std::sort and .NET.
Quicksort is not stable (equal elements may be reordered).
Dual-pivot quicksort (Yaroslavskiy) is used in Java's Arrays.sort().
Quicksort's cache efficiency makes it faster than mergesort despite same complexity.
